name: Value selection bias
statement: Value selection bias is the tendency to answer a diagnostic reasoning problem with a number printed in it rather than one worked out from it.
meaning: The claim is about where a wrong answer comes from rather than about arithmetic going wrong. A diagnostic reasoning problem gives a sample of people, how many have a condition, how many test positive, and how the two overlap. It then asks for the positive predictive value: of those who test positive, how many have the condition. The denominator has to be the total who test positive. Talboy and Schneider report that readers who could not see which total was wanted rarely miscalculated. They answered with a figure already on the page, most often the size of the whole sample, and the name covers that substitution of selection for computation. It is a hypothesis about the shape of errors in one task, tested by coding which value each participant used as a denominator across eight problems. The term belongs to one laboratory. It was set out in a doctoral dissertation in 2019, published in a journal in 2022, and picked up since by two preprints about artificial intelligence, one of them by the same author. English Wikipedia lists it among cognitive biases and has no article on it.

origin.where: University of South Florida doctoral dissertation
origin.note: The phrase appears as hypothesis H2 in Talboy's dissertation Reference Dependence in Bayesian Reasoning, dated March 2019: uninitiated reasoners will select values as presented in the problem rather than compute the correct response. The peer-reviewed version, written with Sandra L. Schneider, reached Frontiers in Psychology on 17 March 2022 and introduces the term as what the authors refer to as a value selection bias. The two documents report the same three experiments on the same 589 students, and the paper adds a fourth study of 364 students that the dissertation does not contain. English Wikipedia's List of cognitive biases gained the entry on 23 March 2023, in an edit by the user Statistress that added the 2022 paper and the authors' 2018 paper in the Journal of Experimental Psychology: Applied as citations.

evidence: Everything published under the name comes from one subject pool at the University of South Florida. Psychology undergraduates worked through eight medical diagnostic problems in supervised computer-lab sessions, without calculators, answering in a frequency format. Experiment 1 used 589 students, after five incomplete records were dropped, spread across ten conditions and reported as three overlapping analyses. In the first, 236 students read either congruent problems, organised around the total who test positive, or incongruent ones, organised around the total who have the condition. Congruent readers were correct on 47% of problems against 33% for incongruent readers, F(1,231) = 9.38, p = 0.002, partial eta squared 0.04. Numeracy tracked accuracy at Spearman r = 0.45. The error coding is the part that names the bias. A participant counted as using a strategy when the same problem value served as the denominator on at least four of the eight problems. Almost every wrong denominator was a number lifted from the problem, and it was usually the overall sample size rather than the competing reference class, p < 0.001 by binomial test in each condition. Reliance on the sample size was similar across the four conditions, chi-square(3, N = 236) = 0.47. In the second analysis, removing the reference class totals so that the correct denominator had to be added up did not lower accuracy, which sat at 46% for congruent and 44% for incongruent pairings with no detectable effect of congruence. One condition broke the pattern. When all organising structure was stripped out, between 25% and 42% of participants computed a denominator instead of choosing one, most by summing the four subsets back into the sample size, and the authors call this the only finding that goes against the bias. Experiment 2 asked where the pull towards the sample size came from. Its 364 students read one of five versions of a problem format the authors had used before. The original wording produced an adjusted 6.42 correct out of eight, or 80%. Adding a sentence asking readers to imagine another random sample of the same size dropped that to 5.0 out of eight, or 63%, p = 0.001, d = 0.60. Reliance on the sample size as the denominator varied across the five versions, chi-square(4, N = 364) = 16.59, p = 0.002, reaching 23% in the new-sample version against about 40% in the comparable condition of the first experiment.

replication.headline: Nobody outside the two authors has tested it: Crossref and Europe PMC record no citations of the paper that names the bias, and Semantic Scholar records two, both preprints about artificial intelligence.
replication.detail: The repetitions that exist are internal. The 2022 paper supports the value selection hypothesis in four analyses, but three of them share one data collection of 589 students and were already reported in the 2019 dissertation. The fourth, with 364 students, is a fresh sample from the same laboratory and the same course-credit pool. Of the two citing works Semantic Scholar lists, one is by Talboy with Elizabeth Fuller and reports a single prompt on which Google Bard answered a mammography question with an incidence rate of 10% instead of a posterior probability, which is an observation about a chatbot rather than a replication. The other cites the 2022 paper in its bibliography. A search for an independent test found none.

limits: The searches for use of the term outside its laboratory covered Crossref bibliographic and title queries, Europe PMC phrase and title queries, PubMed, OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar, English Wikipedia and web search. Europe PMC returns one record for the phrase in a title, the 2022 paper. PubMed's quoted-phrase index does not hold the phrase at all, although its record for that paper carries it in the title, so the paper is reachable there by author rather than by phrase. Google Scholar was not searched. The evidence has narrow edges. It rests on volunteers from one university's psychology courses, on eight medical problems with a frequency response, and on sessions where no calculator was allowed. There is no effect size for the bias itself, because it is a claim about which errors occur rather than about a difference between conditions, and the numbers above are accuracies and chi-square tests. The proportion of participants using each wrong denominator is drawn in bar charts, and the figures quoted here are the ones the running text states: about 40%, 23%, and the range of 25% to 42%. Other condition proportions were not read off the charts. The authors' two 2018 papers were obtained only as abstracts, both being paywalled, and neither abstract uses the phrase. The dissertation was read in full as a PDF from the University of South Florida repository.
misreadings: The first error is to hear selection bias in the statistical sense. That is a property of how a sample was drawn, and it has its own entry here. This is a property of how a person answers a question, and the shared word carries nothing across. The second is to read the Wikipedia gloss as unconditional. It says people rely on numerical data in a problem even where calculation is required, and the authors' own no-organisation condition shows the limit: when no printed value could plausibly be the answer, a quarter to two fifths of participants added four subsets together instead. Talboy and Schneider put the tendency down to reasoners being unsure how to reach the solution rather than to an aversion to arithmetic. The third is to treat this as base-rate neglect or denominator neglect, both of which have their own entries. Those describe what a reasoner does with a prior or a ratio. Value selection bias describes where the number came from, and the number people most often chose was the total sample size, which is not a base rate. The fourth is to read the accuracy figures the authors are best known for as evidence for the bias. The 93% and 87% consistent accuracy reported in their 2018 papers come from aligning the problem's reference class with the question, and those abstracts do not name this bias. The fifth is to count the artificial intelligence preprints as independent support. One is by the author who coined the term.

sources.text: Talboy, A. N., & Schneider, S. L. (2022). Reference Dependence in Bayesian Reasoning: Value Selection Bias, Congruence Effects, and Response Prompt Sensitivity. Frontiers in Psychology, 13, article 729285. The paper that names the bias in the peer-reviewed literature. Read in full as the Europe PMC full-text XML and checked again against the publisher's HTML.

Talboy, A. N. (2019). Reference Dependence in Bayesian Reasoning. USF Tampa Graduate Theses and Dissertations, University of South Florida. The earliest use of the phrase located here, dated March 2019, where it is hypothesis H2. Read in full as the repository PDF.

Talboy, A. N., & Schneider, S. L. (2018). Focusing on what matters: Restructuring the presentation of Bayesian reasoning problems. Journal of Experimental Psychology: Applied, 24(4), 440-458. One of the two works English Wikipedia cites for the term. Paywalled; read only as the abstract in the PubMed record, which reports 93% consistent accuracy on positive predictive value questions with aligned reference classes and does not use the phrase.

Talboy, A. N., & Schneider, S. L. (2018). Improving Understanding of Diagnostic Test Outcomes. Medical Decision Making, 38(5), 573-583. Paywalled; read only as the abstract in the PubMed record, which reports 87% consistent identification of the positive predictive value under a congruent test-focused format.

Wikipedia contributors. List of cognitive biases. English Wikipedia. Cited as the object of study rather than as evidence: it is where the term acquired standing outside its laboratory. The wikitext, the adding revision of 23 March 2023 and its diff were read through the MediaWiki API.

Talboy, A. N., & Fuller, E. (2023). Challenging the appearance of machine intelligence: Cognitive bias in LLMs and Best Practices for Adoption. arXiv preprint. One of two works Semantic Scholar records as citing the 2022 paper. Read in full as the arXiv PDF; its value selection example is a single mammography prompt answered by Google Bard.

Blind Spots and Biases: Exploring the Role of Annotator Cognitive Biases in NLP (2024). arXiv preprint. The other work Semantic Scholar records as citing the 2022 paper, which it lists in its bibliography. Read as the arXiv HTML of version 1.
